solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Attack American behind trouble

parts.note: in American slang the backside is the ass
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: An American is attacked from behind by some trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American behind' is one piece: the US word for a bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is to assault, so it is a synonym of the verb attack.

clue.text: Someone important, such as Sturgeon?

definitions.meaning: the sturgeon is a large fish; Nicola Sturgeon was Scotland's First Minister, a political heavyweight

explanation.surface: Nicola Sturgeon, former First Minister of Scotland, is held up as an important figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a person of influence, while a sturgeon is literally a large fish.

clue.text: Moralising nun sees to it fussily

indicators.note: done fussily, the letters are fiddled about into a new order

explanation.surface: A preachy nun busies herself attending to things.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentential and preachy writing that lectures on morals is pompously moralising: a synonym.

clue.text: Island briefly a part of US

parts.note: IOW is the short form of the Isle of Wight, an English island

explanation.surface: An island is said, in short, to be a part of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: The Midwestern state is one region of the United States of America.

clue.text: Proud Agra, torn apart

indicators.note: torn apart, the letters are pulled to pieces and reassembled

explanation.surface: The proud Indian city of Agra is torn apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A haughty, conceited person is proud in the bad sense: a synonym.

clue.text: Sentimental tosh about bloke in charge

indicators.note: the word for tosh goes about, around, the word for bloke

parts.note: tosh is nonsense, rot
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: Someone talks sentimental tosh about the man in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic feelings are tender and sentimental ones: a near synonym.

clue.text: Position in which Emma might be, never having married?

definitions.text: Position in which Emma might be
definitions.meaning: Emma, the Jane Austen novel, sits on a bookshelf
an old idiom for a woman thought past the chance of marriage

explanation.surface: Emma, a woman who has never married, is pictured in her situation.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma looks like a person, but the first reading takes her as Austen's book.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone left unmarried, like an unsold item still kept in storage.

clue.text: Applause from Cockney joiner

indicators.note: Cockney speech drops the initial H, so the word for applause loses it

parts.note: a hand is a round of applause

explanation.surface: A carpenter from the East End of London gets a round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the East London accent known for dropping H.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjunction links words, so it is a joiner in the grammatical sense.

clue.text: Two renegades heading north, one from central Asia

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards, backwards
two calls for the word for renegade to appear twice

parts.note: a rat is a traitor or renegade

explanation.surface: A pair of turncoats flee north, one of them from Central Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tatars, or Tartars, are a Turkic people of the central Asian steppes.

clue.text: Womaniser exposed in crybaby Ronaldo's letters

indicators.note: the name is laid bare inside the run of words that follows
the letters of the words that follow are where it is found

explanation.surface: A footballer, the crybaby Ronaldo, is shown up as a womaniser by his letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron, the Romantic poet, was a famous seducer, so he stands for a womaniser.

clue.text: Hotel has old approach? Not at all

parts.note: an inn is a hotel
a way is an approach or route

explanation.surface: A hotel keeps an old-fashioned approach, someone asks, and the reply is no.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic negative meaning 'by no means'.

clue.text: Fighter finding diplomat adorable, if a little withdrawn

indicators.note: a little is pulled out of the clue's phrase, a stretch drawn from its letters

explanation.surface: A fighter finds a diplomat adorable, though slightly reserved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'withdrawn' reads as shy, but it means a small piece is drawn out of the text.
explanation.definitionFit: The bullfighter who kills the bull is a kind of fighter.

clue.text: Something biting you, you say? Run for it!

indicators.note: spoken, the insect's name is heard the same

parts.note: a flea is an insect that bites

explanation.surface: Someone warns that something is biting you and urges you to run.
explanation.definitionFit: To escape quickly is to run away: a synonym of the command to bolt.

clue.text: Curiously, opiate isn't something you find in pot

indicators.note: arranged curiously, the letters fall into an odd new order

explanation.surface: Strangely, the drug in your pot is not an opiate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pot' tempts as cannabis; it is a flowerpot.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-leaved Christmas plant is commonly grown in a flowerpot.

clue.text: Recently having sex with Doris?

parts.note: 'the other' is British slang for sex, as in a bit of the other
Doris Day, the American singer and actress

explanation.surface: Someone recently slept with a woman called Doris.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase refers to an occasion a few days ago, so it means lately.

clue.text: How Humpty Dumpty ended up mad?

definitions.meaning: the nursery-rhyme egg fell from the wall he sat on

explanation.surface: A question asks whether Humpty Dumpty ended up crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means wildly unconventional, and literally describes a fall from a wall.

clue.text: Posh chap from Home Counties making you explode

parts.note: SE, the South East of England, where the Home Counties around London lie
a toff is an upper-class man

explanation.surface: An upper-class man from near London makes you lose your temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb is to detonate it, so the phrasal verb means to blow up.

clue.text: Kind of tights in which Molly might be found

definitions.text: in which Molly might be found
definitions.meaning: a molly is a small aquarium fish, which could be caught in a mesh

explanation.surface: A woman called Molly is pictured wearing a particular kind of tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Molly looks like a woman's name, but here she is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-mesh tights are named after the netting used to catch fish.

clue.text: Break silence about enemy leader? She might get you shot!

indicators.note: the rearranged silence goes about, around, the enemy's first letter
breaking the word up lets its letters be rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone breaks a silence about the enemy's leader and fears being shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' suggests a firing squad, but it is a shot of spirits at the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub's licence holder is the landlord or landlady, who serves you drinks such as shots.

clue.text: Check on the Speaker's favourite, a horny creature

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain

indicators.note: as the speaker says it, the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a dear is a darling or favourite

explanation.surface: The Speaker of the House checks on a favourite, a lustful character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horny' suggests lust; it means having antlers.
explanation.definitionFit: The antlered Arctic deer is literally a creature with horns.

clue.text: Index of flirtatious activity?

definitions.meaning: the FTSE 100 share index, nicknamed after its initials
touching someone's feet with yours under the table

explanation.surface: Someone asks about an index of flirting.
explanation.walkthrough: The FTSE is the London stock market index, a natural nod in the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of the London share index coincides with the word for flirting with feet.

clue.text: Idiot ambassador's dress

parts.note: a clot is a fool
HE, His Excellency, the form of address for an ambassador

explanation.surface: A foolish envoy's choice of dress is described.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone is to put clothes on them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Exonerates tragic figure employed in civil service

indicators.note: the tragic figure is put to work inside the abbreviation

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic hero

explanation.surface: A tragic figure working in the civil service is found innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear someone is to declare them blameless, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Right in the middle of decorating? You'll get covered in muck

indicators.note: the letters for right sit in the middle of the abbreviation

parts.note: DIY, do-it-yourself, home decorating and repairs

explanation.surface: Anyone in the middle of decorating ends up mucky.
explanation.definitionFit: Being soiled with grime or filth is an exact synonym.

clue.text: Bugged editor seduced by crackpot Leninist

indicators.note: crackpot means crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor is seduced by a mad Leninist.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug a room is to eavesdrop; past tense, the phrasal verb matches.

clue.text: Harry's bride, heartless and cruel

indicators.note: the central letters of the name are taken away

parts.note: Meghan Markle married Prince Harry

explanation.surface: Prince Harry's wife is accused of being heartless and cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasty, unkind person is called mean: a synonym of unkind.

clue.text: Details somewhat revolutionary?

indicators.note: turned round as in a revolution, so read backwards

parts.note: 'a tad' means somewhat, a little

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the details are somewhat revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Information and facts are data; the plural noun matches.

clue.text: Paying great attention, much like Prince Charles?

definitions.meaning: Charles was long mocked for his prominent ears

explanation.surface: Someone is listening closely, much like Prince Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means listening eagerly, and literally suggests someone with big ears.

clue.text: Can seem to be bottomless

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom letter is cut off

parts.note: to look is to seem

explanation.surface: A tin can seems to have no bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb or a tin; it is US slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are slang for a toilet.

clue.text: Model with walk like a duck? Rubbish!

parts.note: the Model T Ford gives T
to waddle is to walk with a duck's rolling gait

explanation.surface: A fashion model walks like a duck, and someone says it is rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense or foolish talk is called twaddle, a synonym of rubbish.

clue.text: Ought Her Majesty to make a joint?

parts.note: should means ought to
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the Queen ought to make a joint, of meat perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The shoulder is the ball-and-socket joint of the arm, and also a joint of meat.

clue.text: Barman in bed, embracing wife

indicators.note: the word for bed holds the letter for wife in its arms

parts.note: a layer is a bed or stratum

explanation.surface: A bartender in bed with his arms round his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' suggests a pub; it means a member of the Bar, the legal profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Barristers are called to the Bar, so a barrister is a member of the legal profession.
